reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Rectal intussusception is an internal telescoping of the rectal wall that does not protrude through the anus, distinct from external (full-thickness) rectal prolapse
It is graded by the Oxford radiological classification according to whether the intussusception is recto-rectal, recto-anal, or descends into the anal canal
Typical presentations are obstructed defecation with a sensation of incomplete evacuation and blockage, and, when the lead point reaches the anal canal, faecal incontinence and mucus leakage
It is strongly associated with solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, where the intussuscepting mucosa is subjected to trauma and ischaemia
Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI is the key investigation, demonstrating the intussusception and any associated rectocele, enterocele, or perineal descent
Internal intussusception is a common finding in asymptomatic individuals, so symptoms must correlate with the radiological grade before intervention
First-line management is conservative with fibre, stool regulation, avoidance of straining, and biofeedback pelvic-floor retraining
Surgery, such as ventral mesh rectopexy or a stapled transanal resection in selected cases, is reserved for high-grade symptomatic intussusception refractory to conservative care
reference.pathophysiology: Rectal intussusception occurs when a segment of the rectal wall invaginates into the lumen of the rectum or anal canal during straining, without protruding externally. Weakness and redundancy of the rectal wall and its supporting attachments, often with a deep pouch of Douglas and pelvic-floor dysfunction, allow the wall to fold in on itself as intrarectal pressure rises. The intussusceptum acts as a lead point that obstructs the outflow of stool, producing a sensation of blockage and incomplete evacuation and prompting further straining, which perpetuates the process. Repeated shearing and impaction of the prolapsing mucosa against the anal canal cause the mucosal ischaemia, ulceration, and fibrosis of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome. When the lead point repeatedly descends into the anal canal it disrupts the sphincter mechanism and produces incontinence.
additionalDifferentials: Rectocele or enterocele causing obstructed defecation
Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome as coexisting pathology
Rectal neoplasm acting as a lead point
additionalInvestigations: Defecating proctography to grade the intussusception (Oxford classification)
Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI to assess associated compartment defects
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for evacuatory function
Endoanal ultrasound where incontinence or sphincter injury is suspected
Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy to exclude a neoplastic lead point and inspect for solitary rectal ulcer
Colonic transit study where slow-transit constipation is considered
redFlags: Rectal bleeding or a mass suggesting neoplasia acting as a lead point
A persistent rectal ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy
Symptoms disproportionate to a low-grade intussusception, prompting a broader assessment
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with conservative management and biofeedback; surgery for well-selected high-grade symptomatic intussusception can improve obstructed defecation and incontinence, but functional results are variable and recurrence and persistent symptoms are recognised, particularly when other pelvic-floor disorders coexist.
pitfalls: Operating on an incidental low-grade intussusception that does not explain the symptoms
Overlooking coexisting anismus or enterocele that will limit surgical benefit
Failing to biopsy a solitary rectal ulcer and missing malignancy
Attributing all evacuatory symptoms to the intussusception when a functional disorder predominates
Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of biofeedback and bowel regulation
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on rectal prolapse and obstructed defecation
Oxford rectal prolapse grading and pelvic-floor imaging literature (source-neutral)
management: First-line conservative management of obstructed defecation with dietary fibre, adequate fluids, laxatives and bowel-habit retraining
Pelvic-floor biofeedback and defecatory retraining to correct dyssynergic straining that perpetuates the intussusception
Treat associated solitary rectal ulcer syndrome with topical therapies and strict avoidance of straining
Reserve surgery, such as ventral mesh rectopexy or stapled transanal rectal resection, for well-selected high-grade symptomatic disease after conservative failure
Ensure symptoms correlate with the radiological Oxford grade before intervention, as internal intussusception is common in asymptomatic people
Multidisciplinary assessment with colorectal surgery, gastroenterology and pelvic-floor physiotherapy, addressing coexisting rectocele, enterocele or perineal descent
